name: Dii (Mbé)
overview: In the majority in the lamidate of Mbé, the Dii live with Fulani, Moundang, Toupouri, Mada, Mafa and Bamiléké. Coming from Mayo-Rey, they found a place of refuge in Mbé. The chiefdom, the circumciser-priest and the blacksmith organise society; circumcision, with its three-day mbé dance, is its great rite.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Majority group, integrated with the Fulani, Moundang, Toupouri, Mada, Mafa and Bamiléké; each keeps their own language, but the children learn the local speech variety.
Dii associations exist in all regions, with no real community elsewhere.
Open group: marriages take place with other peoples.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: Ancestral land that belongs to them, a former place of refuge and resettlement.
Having set out from Mayo-Rey, they stayed in several places (Gbaha Sa, Gbada Sat, Gbaha Iraawa), which they have left entirely.
The Dii and the Gbaya allied in times of war.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: The chiefdom (chief and notables), the circumcising priest and the blacksmith structure society.
A crier rings the bell to summon the men; notables and wise men reach a consensus that they submit to the chief.
The Dii of Mbé have relatives among the Dii of Karna.
Princes share the ritual functions, rotating among themselves: the ndmoɔna group buries the chief; others lead the circumcision cult.
Formerly, a woman did not go too near men, and children did not hold out their hand to adults.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; exogamy, especially male, avoids incest; the wife joins her husband's family.
The boy becomes a man through circumcision; the girl, through marriage.
The boy's family asks for her hand, and the suitor performs services for his future in-laws; formerly, the girl stayed with her future mother-in-law to prepare herself there.
The bride price, today in money, formerly consisted of black cloth and a hoe; an ox was slaughtered and shared, which brought honour to the wife.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: Ancestor cult led by the circumcision priest in case of misfortune; annual sacrifices (in November) for the objects of circumcision.
Sacred places: tɸ́, the place of circumcision on the riverbank, a memory of the group's history; ɗàwá, near the river, where ritual objects are sacrificed.
Birth may be the return of a forebear; death, a return to the forebears or a divine punishment, depending on the circumstances. When displeased, the dead transmit messages.
Formerly, the circumcised boy no longer went to the kitchen or carried water, and girls did not wear trousers.
Witchcraft and theft were judged by ritual ordeals, abandoned with Christianity; each village had at least two deities consulted by the chief.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men: farming, trade, livestock rearing. Women: trade (wine, fritters), hairdressing, weaving.
The land belongs to the village chief; one goes through the lamido.
Ancestral crafts: hunting bows and arrows, axes, fosi for cutting roof thatch, hoes, mortars.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Woven boubou, gandoura, wrappers.
Traditional medicine remains massively used, quick and economical.
Beauty, for both sexes, lies in speech and conduct.
Courtship: gifts and respect for the in-laws; the woman respects her husband.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: The mbé (drum and two bells) is danced for three days during circumcision; the napdii (drum and bell) accompanies weddings and the sharing of millet.
String instruments: kɔŋ ha, small guitar with 8-12 strings and little bells; kɔŋ naŋ, one-metre harp.
The ADECAM festival, every two years, brought together all the dances of the district.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: By its sociopolitical organisation, the group recalls the peoples of the Grassfields.

sections.title: The names
items: Twins' names: Housseini and Hassana for boys, Haimata for girls.
When the cord fell off, the father sacrificed a cockerel or an ox on the family altar; today, kola is shared and the name is given.
One does not change name, but one receives a pseudonym; the father is called bàʔá, the eldest bàní, and the younger sibling is called by name.
The founding ancestor, Dzúbérú Kùmbà, is “the one who withdraws into himself”.

lessons.title: Who are the Dii (Mbé)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Dii (Mbé) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Dii (Mbé) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Dii (Mbé) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Dii (Mbé) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Dii (Mbé) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Dii (Mbé) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Majority group, integrated with the Fulani, Moundang, Toupouri, Mada, Mafa and Bamiléké; each keeps its own language, but the children learn the local speech variety. • Dii associations exist in all regions, with no real community elsewhere. • Open group: marriages take place with other peoples. • Ancestral land that belongs to them, a former place of refuge and resettlement. • Having left Mayo-Rey, they stayed in several places (Gbaha Sa, Gbada Sat, Gbaha Iraawa), which they left entirely.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: In the majority in the lamidate of Mbé, the Dii live with Fulani, Moundang, Toupouri, Mada, Mafa and Bamiléké. Coming from Mayo-Rey, they found a place of refuge in Mbé. The chiefdom, the circumciser-priest and the blacksmith organise society; circumcision, with its three-day mbé dance, is its great rite.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Dii (Mbé) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Power and social organisation among the Dii (Mbé)
lessons.anelcac: Socio-political organisation, rules for living together
lessons.competence: Describe how the Dii (Mbé) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.
lessons.situation: An important decision must be made for the whole Dii (Mbé) village. Who decides, and how?
lessons.materiel: The community's cultural profile, paper and felt-tip pens for the organisation chart.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe how the Dii (Mbé) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “An important decision has to be made for the whole Dii (Mbé) village. Who decides, and how?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who holds authority? — How are decisions made (consensus, vote, the chief's decision)? — What rules of respect and deference are observed? — Which groups or societies play a particular role?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Chiefdom (chief and notables), circumcision priest and blacksmith structure society. • A crier rings the bell to summon the men; notables and elders reach a consensus which they submit to the chief. • The Dii of Mbé have relatives among the Dii of Karna. • Princes share out the ritual functions, which they rotate among themselves: the ndmoɔna group buries the chief; others lead the circumcision cult. • In the past, a woman did not go too near men, and children did not offer their hand to adults.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The chiefdom (chief and notables), the circumcising priest and the blacksmith structure society. A town crier rings the bell to summon the men; notables and elders reach a consensus which they submit to the chief. The Dii of Mbé have relatives among the Dii of Karna.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a diagram (organisation chart) of power among the Dii (Mbé), then explain in 3 sentences how a decision is made.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Dii (Mbé)
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Dii (Mbé), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Dii (Mbé).
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Dii (Mbé), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Dii (Mbé).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: cassava leaves (kpak gbaj), melon leaves (limam), garam (red fruits), sii (fried groundnut flour). • Drinks: bil-bil, balɔŋ, ɗadi. • Men: farming, trade, livestock rearing. Women: trade (wine, fritters), hairdressing, weaving. • Ancestral crafts: hunting bows and arrows, axes, fosi for cutting roof thatch, hoes, mortars.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Dii (Mbé) eat mainly cassava leaves, melon leaves, garam, sii. Traditional drinks: bil-bil, balɔŋ, ɗadi. These foods are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Dii (Mbé): write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Birth, name and the passage to adulthood among the Dii (Mbé)
objectives: Explain the meaning of a birth

vocabulary.frenchText: “the chief of the hill of fires”

lessons.competence: Explain how the Dii (Mbé) welcome a child, give the child a name and mark the child's entry into adulthood.
lessons.situation: A child has just been born in a Dii (Mbé) family. How will he be named, and how will he become an adult?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain how the Dii (Mbé) welcome a child, give it a name and mark its entry into adulthood.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A child has just been born in a Dii (Mbé) family. How will they be named, and how will they become an adult?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What does a birth mean for the community? — Who gives the name, when and how? — Can the name change during a lifetime? — When and how does one become a man or a woman?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Twin names: Housseini and Hassana for boys, Haimata for girls. • When the umbilical cord fell off, the father sacrificed a cockerel or an ox on the family altar; today, kola is shared and the name is given. • One does not change name, but receives a nickname; one says bàʔá to the father, bàní to the eldest, and calls the younger by name. • Birth may be the return of an ancestor; death, a return to the ancestors or a divine punishment, depending on circumstances. When displeased, the dead transmit messages. • The boy becomes a man through circumcision; the young woman, through marriage.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Twins' names: Housseini and Hassana for boys, Haimata for girls. One does not change one's name, but one receives a pseudonym; the father is called bàʔá, the eldest bàní, and the younger sibling is called by name.

steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who chooses the spouse? Do people marry within the group or outside it? — What are the stages of marriage? — What does the bride price include, and what does each item symbolise? — Where does the couple live after the marriage?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The mbé (tam-tam and two bells) is danced for three days during circumcision; the napdii (tam-tam and bell) accompanies weddings and the sharing of millet. • String instruments: kɔŋ ha, a small guitar with 8-12 strings and little bells; kɔŋ naŋ, a one-metre harp. • The ADECAM festival, every two years, brought together all the dances of the subdivision.

steps.instruction: Among the Dii (Mbé), traditional dances (mbé, napdii) accompany the major moments of life: festivals, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: drum, bells, kɔŋ ha, kɔŋ naŋ. Festival(s): ADECAM festival, circumcision.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Dii (Mbé)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Dii (Mbé), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Dii (Mbé). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Dii (Mbé), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Dii (Mbé)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Dii (Mbé), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Dii (Mbé). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Dii (Mbé), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Dii (Mbé). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Ancestor worship led by the circumcision priest in case of misfortune; annual sacrifices (in November) for the circumcision objects. • Sacred places: tɸ́, the circumcision site on the riverbank, a memory of the group's history; ɗàwá, near the river, where the ritual objects are sacrificed. • A birth may be the return of an ancestor; death, a return to the ancestors or a divine punishment, depending on the circumstances. When displeased, the dead send messages. • In the past, the circumcised man no longer went to the kitchen or carried water, and girls did not wear trousers. • Witchcraft and theft were judged by ritual ordeals, abandoned with Christianity; each village had at least two deities consulted by the chief.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Ancestor cult led by the circumcision priest in case of misfortune; annual sacrifices (in November) for the objects of circumcision. Sacred places: tɸ́, the place of circumcision on the riverbank, memory of the group's history; ɗàwá, near the river, where ritual objects are sacrificed.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Dii (Mbé) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Dii
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Dii (Mbé) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Dii (Mbé) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Dii (Mbé) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Dii (Mbé) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • The community's language is Dii. • Greeting formulae: Dza᷅ma᷅ vi᷇na᷇nna᷅ = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); U᷅tna᷇nna᷅ mɔ᷅ = morning greeting (one person); Vi᷇u᷅tna᷇nna᷅ = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: ɗaga, I᷇du᷇, Ta᷇nnə᷇, ɗa᷅ru᷇, Nu᷄nu᷄. • The founding ancestor, Dzúbérú Kùmbà, is “the one who withdraws into himself”. • By its sociopolitical organisation, the group recalls the peoples of the Grassfields.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Dii are the first steps towards communicating with the Dii (Mbé). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.
